items.title: Battery Vessels Could Help Electrify Most of Global Shipping Emissions
items.original_title: Battery Vessels Could Help Electrify Most of Global Shipping Emissions
items.summary: Battery-electric ships are economical only if the pack is cycled frequently, so they have been confined to short-sea, ferry and harbour vessels rather than the infrequently-berthing deep-sea fleet. Dedicated battery vessels (BVs) remove this limit by separating the battery from the host: coupling at or near a port and returning to port to recharge, they keep their packs cycling across many hosts. Using a gridded shipping- CO2 field and a geometric relay-corridor servability model, we map the global share BVs could serve. On a denominator of all shipping CO2(e), the battery-addressable share is about 62%, its servable corridors concentrated in European–Mediterranean and East and Southeast Asian waters. A screening cost model puts BV-delivered energy at breakeven with fuel oil near $173/tCO2e (well-to-wake basis) for a 20MW host and a future $100/kWh battery pack price, falling as host power rises. The maritime economy enters the latter part of 2026 after another period of disruption and adjustment. It carries more than 80% of world trade by volume¹ and remains the most energy-efficient way to move goods over long distances. Its ability to adapt has again demonstrated the central role of maritime transport in the global economy. Global goods trade reached approximately USD 13.7 trillion in the first half of 2026, an increase of 12.5% compared with the same period in 2025.

Representing the global commercial shipping fleet, the associations urged governments to agree on effective and enforceable global regulations that provide investment certainty, incentivise cleaner fuels and maintain a level playing field across international shipping. Container shipping and vehicle carriers have committed more than USD $200 billion to over 1,350 dual-fuel ships, including over 500 already operating. An agreement that delivers all three can accelerate progress towards net zero and help turn the investment already underway into real emissions reductions.” WSC cautions that further delays or a framework focused primarily on experience building or fuel market readiness would prolong uncertainty rather than support the transition.

items.title: HMM signs green shipping deal with Nextpower
items.original_title: HMM signs green shipping deal with Nextpower
items.summary: South Korean shipping company HMM said Monday it had signed a deal allowing US solar technology company Nextpower to reflect emissions reductions from HMM’s use of lower-carbon marine fuels in its supply chain emissions reporting. Under its Green Sailing Service, HMM uses lower-carbon fuels and passes the resulting emissions reductions on to cargo customers for use in their Scope 3 reporting, which covers indirect emissions across a company’s value chain. The agreements allow HMM to recover part of the cost of using lower-carbon fuels, helping fund further investments in lower-emission shipping. Reductions made to comply with regulations, including those in the European Union, are ineligible. HMM uses independent third-party verification to check the reported reductions and help avoid double counting, which occurs when more than one company claims the same reduction. Customers can use the verified figures in their environmental, social and governance disclosures. The Nextpower agreement follows similar deals with German logistics company Hellmann in 2023, Swedish furniture retailer Ikea in 2024 and US sportswear company Nike in 2025. We plan to continue investing in greenhouse gas reductions, including diversifying our use of low-carbon fuels,” an HMM official said. “We aim to develop our environmental initiatives into a new driver of growth.” Source: The Korea Heralde

items.title: Tanker boom turns conservative owners into asset traders
items.original_title: Tanker boom turns conservative owners into asset traders
items.summary: Surging tanker and VLGC values are turning some of shipping’s most conservative owners into opportunistic asset players, with a string of recent sales generating extraordinary returns in a matter of months. The disruption caused by the Strait of Hormuz crisis has sent secondhand values soaring, creating lucrative opportunities for owners and traders who acquired ships before prices took off. Malaysia’s MISC, traditionally regarded as one of shipping’s more conservative owners, is reportedly selling the 21-year-old shuttle tanker Jasmine Knutsen to Indonesian interests. In September, Trafigura Maritime acquired the Samsung-built suezmax Seaways Sabine from International Seaways for approximately $74m, some $53m above what the US-listed owner originally paid for the vessel when new. Just two months later, the same tanker, renamed Sponde, was reported sold again for around $110m. If confirmed, the transaction would deliver Trafigura a gross gain of approximately $36m in barely eight weeks. BW has also joined the selling spree, recently offloading the 83,134 cu m VLGC BW Mistral for well over $100m. Acquired as part of BW’s purchase of John Fredriksen-controlled Avance Gas’s VLGC fleet less than two years ago, the vessel is understood to have generated a gain of approximately $37m. With secondhand values reaching exceptional levels, the distinction between traditional shipowners and speculative asset traders is becoming increasingly blurred.

items.title: Spain joins growing global crackdown on scrubbers
items.original_title: Spain joins growing global crackdown on scrubbers
items.summary: Spain has become the latest country to clamp down on ship scrubbers, announcing a nationwide ban on washwater discharges in ports and designated coastal waters from July 1, 2027. Unlike countries that have initially targeted open-loop systems, Spain’s new royal decree covers open-loop, closed-loop and hybrid scrubbers from day one. The restrictions apply to all merchant vessels, regardless of flag, operating in Spanish internal maritime waters, port areas and designated anchorages within territorial waters. Ships will not have to remove their scrubbers but must switch to compliant low-sulphur fuel or retain wastewater onboard for subsequent disposal ashore. Spain’s decision goes beyond last year’s OSPAR agreement, which requires northeast Atlantic countries to ban open-loop discharges in ports and internal waters by July 2027, extending to all scrubber types in 2029. Denmark, Sweden and Finland banned open-loop discharges in their territorial waters in July 2025, with restrictions on closed-loop systems following in 2029. Greenland’s parliament voted last month to introduce a phased ban, starting in July 2027. Scrubbers have become increasingly controversial since the IMO’s global sulphur cap took effect in 2020. Spain says scrubber washwater can contain heavy metals and organic pollutants and contribute to marine acidification.

One case illustrates the pattern end to end: On June 9, about 130,400 barrels of Russian diesel was loaded at Taman onto a Russian-flagged tanker sanctioned under Russia programs. items.original_title: Spain to ban all scrubber wastewater discharge in its ports
items.summary: Spain has banned ships from discharging wastewater from any type of scrubber in its ports and anchorages from 1 July 2027 to protect the marine environment, the transport ministry said. Spain’s Council of Ministers approved the royal decree on Tuesday. It applies to all civilian ships fitted with scrubbers, whatever their flag, and covers open-loop, closed-loop and hybrid systems alike. Spain’s move complies with the OSPAR Commission’s decision agreed in June last year, under which 15 European governments and the EU agreed to stop ships from discharging scrubber washwater in ports and internal waters. Each OSPAR member must ban discharges from open-loop scrubbers in internal waters and ports by 1 July 2027, and from scrubbers in any mode by 1 July 2029. Spain’s decision brings forward the ban on closed-loop and hybrid scrubbers by two years and extends the ban to areas outside those covered by the OSPAR decision. Class society DNV said in July last year that whether to extend the ban to the Mediterranean would be up to Spain and France. There are currently 7,230 ships equipped with scrubbers across the world, with the number expected to increase to 7,612 vessels by 2029, according to DNV data. Denmark, Sweden and Finland banned open-loop discharges in their territorial waters from 1 July 2025.

items.title: Vessel renewal incentive policy in China: Potential greenhouse gas reduction impact and opportunities for improvement
items.original_title: Vessel renewal incentive policy in China: Potential greenhouse gas reduction impact and opportunities for improvement
items.summary: Maritime shipping plays a key role in China’s national freight sector, accounting for over 50% of transportation activity in 2024. Decarbonization of this sector at a rate in line with the government’s goal to achieve carbon neutrality before 2060 will require the large-scale application of ships fueled by low- and zero-carbon fuels. China introduced policies in 2024 to promote the scrapping and renewal of old ships, which offer shipowners tiered subsidies to renew older ships before their mandatory retirement dates, with greater support for new/clean energy vessels (NCEVs). This paper estimates the potential impact of the retire-and-renew (RNR) policy on fleet renewal and greenhouse gas emissions in China’s coastal fleet. Using the Vessel Economic Guidance and Assessment (VEGA) model and Polaris, a shipping emissions projection model, we estimated fleet renewal and greenhouse gas emissions from 2025 to 2050 under the existing RNR policy design and two alternative scenarios. Key findings • The RNR policy would accelerate fleet renewal and result in additional NCEVs being introduced into the fleet. • Increasing the subsidy level without other supporting policies would lead to up to 17.4% higher well-to-wake greenhouse gas emissions between 2025 and 2050. • Combining a carbon pricing mechanism, an e-fuel blending mandate, and incentive support for e-fuels would help to jumpstart both NCEV adoption and e-fuel uptake.

In a regulatory filing on Nov. 19, Hanwha Ocean said it had signed a shipbuilding contract worth a total of 364.2 billion won ($262.06 million). Including this contract, Hanwha Ocean has recorded orders for a total of 47 vessels (cases) so far this year. Its cumulative order value has reached about $8.54 billion, a solid trend that exceeds market expectations. The tally includes 24 VLCCs, eight liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers, six container ships, three Very Large Ammonia Carriers (VLACs), and three Very Large Gas Carriers (VLGCs). In particular, the orders are led by eco-friendly vessels aligned with the carbon-neutral trend, special-purpose ships, and Wind Turbine Installation Vessels (WTIVs), all of which require highly advanced shipbuilding technology. Industry experts say Hanwha Ocean is focusing on selectively winning orders centered on high-profit vessel types rather than simply expanding order volume. The VLCC market requires high technological entry barriers and large-scale facilities, and Hanwha Ocean is solidifying its market dominance based on accumulated construction experience.

items.title: India scraps compulsory retirement age for ships
items.original_title: India scraps compulsory retirement age for ships
items.summary: India has scrapped compulsory retirement ages for ships flying its flag, reversing a policy designed to push older tonnage out of the country’s merchant fleet. The Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) issued a new order this week 18 allowing existing Indian-flagged vessels to continue trading regardless of age, provided they meet prescribed technical and safety standards. The government has also relaxed restrictions on bringing older vessels onto the Indian register. Tankers, bulk carriers and general cargo ships over 20 years old can now be considered for registration, subject to a technical review and approval process. For containerships, gas carriers and chemical tankers, the corresponding threshold is 25 years. The latest move overturns restrictions introduced in 2023 and revised in January this year, which had imposed firm age limits on ships entering and remaining in the Indian fleet. The revised standards also extend to foreign-flagged ships operating in India’s coastal trade under the Coastal Shipping Act 2025. They do not impose a general age restriction on every foreign ship making an international port call in India. The relaxation could help owners seeking to transfer older ships to the Indian flag, including containerline MSC, whose previously announced plan to register about a dozen vessels in India had reportedly encountered difficulties under the earlier age rules.

items.original_title: Smart Sea urges shipowners to tackle ageing infrastructure before investing in new digital solutions
items.summary: Shipowners risk undermining their digitalisation efforts by investing in new technology while continuing to operate outdated and potentially vulnerable IT systems, according to maritime technology consultancy SmartSea. Recent fleet assessments by the company have identified vessels still running unsupported operating systems, including Windows 7, raising concerns over cybersecurity, system reliability and the ability to integrate modern digital applications. Kris Vedat, CEO of Smart Sea, warns that too many operators are prioritising new software and connectivity over the infrastructure needed to support them. There’s little point investing in sophisticated technology if the underlying systems aren’t fit for purpose.” Mr Vedat believes the industry needs to move away from short-term technology fixes towards a more co-ordinated approach that includes infrastructure assessments, standardised processes and phased implementation. Technology investments should be judged on the operational value they deliver, not simply the immediate cost savings.” The lack of consistent technical standards across shipping adds to the challenge, particularly for third-party ship managers inheriting vessels with ageing IT and operational technology. Smart Sea believes clearer minimum standards would help improve cybersecurity and support more effective fleet-wide digitalisation. Mr Vedat believes addressing these technical and commercial barriers is essential if shipping is to realise the full potential of digitalisation, automation and decarbonisation technologies.

Local 26 represents approximately 250 watchmen responsible for security duties, including checking credentials at terminal entrances and conducting patrols. Yesterday, the PMA claimed the union had made little progress towards accepting its proposals and was unwilling to extend the current contract beyond 12:01 am on 21 November. items.title: US ethanol offers lower GHG abatement costs than methanol, ammonia: study
items.original_title: US ethanol offers lower GHG abatement costs than methanol, ammonia: study
items.summary: US corn-based ethanol could offer shipowners a cheaper route to reducing greenhouse gas emissions than low-carbon methanol and ammonia, potentially opening a new marine fuel market for American producers as the global fleet of methanol-capable vessels expands, according to a study released last week. Ethanol could abate about 2.09 metric tons of CO2 equivalent for every $1,000 spent on fuel, compared with 1.30 mt for low-carbon methanol and 1.73 mt for low-carbon ammonia, the Maritime Ethanol & Methanol Alliance, an initiative by the nonprofit Global Centre for Green Fuels, said in the study. MEMA estimated ethanol’s well-to-wake greenhouse gas intensity at 34.9 grams of CO2e/megajoule, compared with 15 gCO2e/MJ for low-carbon methanol and 10 gCO2e/MJ for low-carbon ammonia. In the study, based on classification society ABS’s technical analysis, MEMA assumed US corn ethanol prices on a free-on-board Houston basis at $750/mt, equivalent to $1,125/mt of very low sulfur fuel oil on an energy-adjusted basis. The study’s indicative mid-2026 prices showed ethanol remained substantially more expensive than conventional bunkers but offered lower costs than other low-carbon alternatives. US ethanol supply The US produced 16.4 billion gallons of ethanol in 2025, against an installed capacity of 18.5 billion gallons/year, leaving about 2 billion gallons of spare capacity, according to the study.

items.title: COSCO port fuels growth in APEC trade
items.original_title: COSCO port fuels growth in APEC trade
items.summary: As leaders and delegates focus on advancing regional economic integration under the framework of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a transformative megaproject on the eastern Pacific coast stands as a powerful testament to these shared goals. Chancay Port in Peru, a vital APEC economy, has rapidly evolved into a pivotal logistics hub connecting Latin America with Asia, breathing life into the vision of a seamlessly interconnected Asia-Pacific. Inaugurated in November 2024, the port was hailed by Chinese President Xi Jinping as the starting point of an Inca Trail of the New Era. By slashing the one-way maritime transit time between Peru and China from roughly 35 days to just 23 days, the deep-water port has reduced logistics costs by more than 20 percent, fundamentally reshaping trans-Pacific trade dynamics. Carlos Aquino, director of the Center for Asian Studies at Peru’s National University of San Marcos, said that if Brazil routes its cargo through Chancay to China, it could save upwards of 15 days in transport time, highlighting the port’s immense geopolitical and economic magnitude. Over the past two years, the port has generated $3.65 billion in import and export trade, handling half a million twenty-foot equivalent units of containers. It is projected to bring $4.5 billion in annual economic benefits to Peru and create over 8,000 direct jobs.

Geopolitics, trade relationships, energy systems and supply chains are being reshaped, meaning the industry may not return to its former operating environment even if some risks ease, Wang told the Xinde Marine Forum in Hong Kong. “Many of today’s changes may not be temporary,” he said. “Rather than waiting for that environment to return, companies must make adaptability and continuity of service part of the long-term management.” Wang’s comments followed executives’ warnings during Hong Kong Maritime Week 2026 that a return to past confidence in safe passage might be difficult. “With the way that cheap disposable weapons, if you like, single-use weapons can be deployed across chokepoints at sea, I think it’s very hard for us to see how we can all be as relaxed as we were in the previous 40 years,” Brown said. The tanker fleet had secured employment for about two-thirds of its Q4 operating days and some operating days in 2027, at freight rates substantially above those achieved in January-September. Shipping as critical infrastructure Brown said resilient voyages required cooperation between governments, navies and commercial shipping, alongside efforts to strengthen ships and crews.

items.title: Shipping industry urges governments to agree on global GHG regulations to provide regulatory certainty and incentivize maritime decarbonization
items.original_title: Shipping industry urges governments to agree on global GHG regulations to provide regulatory certainty and incentivize maritime decarbonization
items.summary: The global shipping industry welcomes continuing efforts by all IMO Member States to agree on a global framework of practical, effective and fit for purpose regulations to help decarbonize international shipping and, whilst further improving energy efficiency, continue striving towards the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy goal of net-zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by or close to 2050. The industry recognizes that all proposals put forward by governments, and the elements these contain, remain under consideration, but emphasizes the importance of an achievable, enforceable, and stable regulatory framework which reflects cost and availability and provides clear incentives for the development and deployment of commercially viable alternative fuels. The regulatory framework must also meaningfully support a safe energy transition through solutions which are data-driven and fuel and technology neutral. The GHG reduction regulations to be adopted by IMO Member States must reward verifiable emission reductions and incentivize, financially and/or technically, further investments that advance maritime decarbonization. In addition, the regulations should also provide optional/flexible compliance mechanisms so that shipping companies, large and small, can manage the transition, recognizing the current unavailability of commercially viable zero/near-zero GHG fuels and technologies (ZNZs) for the majority of the existing fleet. Continued industry investment and effective implementation will depend on global regulatory certainty and the reliable production and cost-competitiveness of alternative fuels at scale.

items.title: Shipping Industry Presses for Global IMO Climate Deal as Divisions Over Rules Persist
items.original_title: Shipping Industry Presses for Global IMO Climate Deal as Divisions Over Rules Persist
items.summary: Nine major shipping associations are urging governments to reach an agreement on global greenhouse gas regulations, warning that continued uncertainty threatens investment in cleaner ships and alternative fuels ahead of critical negotiations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO). The joint statement , issued Wednesday, calls for practical, enforceable and globally consistent rules that would give shipowners and fuel suppliers the certainty needed to invest in maritime decarbonization. The appeal comes as governments prepare to revisit the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, whose formal adoption was postponed in October 2025 amid opposition from the United States and several oil-producing countries. The nine organizations—including BIMCO, the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), INTERTANKO, INTERCARGO and the World Shipping Council (WSC)—reaffirmed their support for the IMO’s goal of achieving net-zero emissions from international shipping by or around 2050. The appeal follows a recent analysis by InfluenceMap that found broad industry support for a global IMO climate agreement, but significant differences over carbon pricing, fuel standards and how emissions from alternative fuels should be calculated. Another point of contention is the relationship between global IMO rules and existing European regulations. The renewed industry push comes ahead of an IMO working group meeting November 23–27, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s MEPC 85 session from November 30 to December 3.

items.title: Geneva Dry: TCC’s Emily Koo on the disconnect between dry bulk rates and asset prices
items.original_title: Geneva Dry: TCC’s Emily Koo on the disconnect between dry bulk rates and asset prices
items.summary: TCC Group’s Emily Koo warns that elevated vessel prices, an overreliance on market statistics and a narrow focus on technology risk distracting dry bulk shipping from the bigger challenges ahead. The growing disconnect between freight rates and vessel prices, and the industry’s tendency to overlook what might go wrong, will be among the key talking points when dry bulk executives gather in Geneva next April, reckons Emily Koo of Hong Kong shipowner TCC Group. Koo, one of more than 50 shipowners to take the stage at Geneva Dry 2027, is concerned that the industry is becoming too focused on explaining freight market rallies through statistics rather than examining the underlying health of the shipping business. She questions how long owners can continue justifying the disconnect between earnings and asset values while “sweeping what might go wrong” under the rug. Koo is group managing director and fourth-generation custodian of Hong Kong’s TCC Group, whose origins date to 1917, when her great-grandfather Koo Chung-shui established the family shipping business in Shanghai. The group subsequently relocated its operations to Hong Kong, building a century-long reputation in dry bulk and tanker shipping. Rather than presentations dominated by familiar market data, she wants to hear how industry leaders interpret the challenges facing dry bulk shipping and how they intend to respond.

However, maritime security firm Vanguard Tech identified it as the Liberian-flagged product tanker NAVIG8 MESSI , which is commercially managed by ADNOC L&S. The gas market remains tight amid curtailed Qatari supplies and the bloc’s depleted gas inventories. Colder weather is forecast across much of Europe, potentially boosting heating demand and accelerating storage withdrawals. Meteorologists also see an increasing likelihood that the earliest-ever recorded breakdown of the polar vortex could send a blast of cold Arctic air southward from the Nordics in late November or early December. items.title: Shipping heavyweights warn against double carbon charges
items.original_title: Shipping heavyweights warn against double carbon charges
items.summary: Nine of the world’s leading shipping associations have joined forces to push governments towards a global emissions deal, warning that a patchwork of regional regulations risks leaving shipowners paying multiple times for the same carbon emissions. The joint intervention comes ahead of a crucial round of talks at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) later this month, with governments still divided over how to regulate and price shipping’s greenhouse gas emissions. BIMCO, the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), Intercargo, Intertanko, the World Shipping Council, Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA), Interferry, the International Bunker Industry Association (IBIA) and the International Parcel Tankers Association (IPTA) have called for a single global framework that applies equally to vessels regardless of flag, ownership or trade. The groups warned that national and regional schemes could result in duplicated compliance requirements and multiple charges for the same emissions, undermining efforts to establish a level playing field. The intervention comes after the IMO failed to secure agreement on its proposed Net-Zero Framework in October 2025, forcing governments to postpone adoption for a year. The industry’s latest appeal follows growing concern over the spread of regional carbon schemes. Several African governments are moving towards their own shipping emissions charges, while European operators already face the EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime regulations.

items.title: Global spot gas prices skyrocket but European buyers should stick to spot-indexation, experts say
items.original_title: Global spot gas prices skyrocket but European buyers should stick to spot-indexation, experts say
items.summary: Europe’s share of LNG imports bought on a spot basis was 36% in 2026 year to date. This compared to 38% in full year 2025 and 35% in full year 2024 according to ICIS data. This means that although oil prices have risen, major LNG buyers in Asia that take most of their LNG on long-term contracts indexed to oil have likely not seen their overall weighted average cost of gas imports rise as much as those in Europe buying almost entirely at spot gas market related prices. The massive increase in European and global spot prices and Europe’s increasing exposure to them has raised two questions: does Europe need to change its purchasing strategy and sign more long-term deals and will that also reopen the debate of oil versus spot indexation in such sale and purchase agreements? During times of more plentiful supply this served Europe well, with spot gas prices looking competitive against oil for the decade from 2010 to 2020. So, should European buyers be looking again at how to index their deals and the comparison between oil and spot gas? Market experts polled by ICIS said the current market dynamics and extremely high spot gas prices are not likely to lead to a new shift towards oil-indexation in long-term deals.

items.original_title: Global crude surplus will reach 2 million b/d in 2027: Goldman Sachs
items.summary: The global oil market is heading for a 2 million barrels/day surplus in 2027 as Persian Gulf liquids output is expected to rise by nearly 4 million b/d above current levels and new pipeline infrastructure will route an increasing share of Gulf supply around the Strait of Hormuz, Goldman Sachs analysts said. The investment bank’s base case projections are underpinned by a sharp recovery already underway in Gulf crude exports, with Goldman Sachs estimating that Gulf crude exports rose 2 million b/d month over month in October, recovering to their 2025 average. That rebound drove a major reversal in global liquids balances, shifting the market from a 600,000 b/d deficit in September to a 1.6 million b/d surplus in October, according to the bank. Goldman Sachs forecasts an additional 3.8 million b/d of pipeline bypass capacity to come online over the next year. By end-2027, this infrastructure build-out should allow Gulf countries to export over 14 million b/d — or around 60% of their 2025 average export volumes — via pipelines bypassing Hormuz alone, Goldman Sachs said. Goldman Sachs said this would help global stocks recover from current low levels, with the 2027 supply-demand surplus, measured as oil production minus oil end-use demand, reaching 2 million b/d.

items.title: UK sets out 2030 marine fuel crackdown
items.original_title: UK sets out 2030 marine fuel crackdown
items.summary: Britain has laid out plans for a new shipping fuel regulation that could initially cover around 5,000 vessels calling at its ports, including ships operating on international routes. The Department for Transport opened a consultation this week on a proposed greenhouse gas intensity standard, which the government expects to introduce from 2030. The regime would initially apply to ships of 5,000 gt and above, irrespective of flag, requiring operators to progressively reduce the lifecycle emissions intensity of the fuels and energy they use. Britain is taking its lead from the EU’s FuelEU Maritime framework, which entered into force in January 2025, while seeking to retain flexibility around future IMO requirements. Government modelling suggests 4,913 vessels of at least 5,000 gt called at UK ports in 2019. Another 2,405 smaller ships could eventually be brought into the regime if the threshold is lowered to 400 gt. The latest move comes after domestic shipping was brought into the UK Emissions Trading Scheme in July. British shipowners have already warned against copying the administrative problems encountered under FuelEU Maritime. In October, the UK Chamber of Shipping called for better-aligned reporting systems and realistic targets reflecting the availability of alternative fuels.

items.summary: BW Group-backed Hafnia has abandoned its pursuit of Danish product tanker rival Torm and is preparing to unwind its near-20% holding after failing to win support for a combination of the two shipping giants. The Oslo- and New York-listed owner said on Wednesday it intends to exit its entire 19.85% stake, preferably by distributing its 20.36m Torm shares to Hafnia shareholders through a special dividend. The holding was valued at $686.6m based on Torm’s November 17 closing share price of $33.73.The move brings an abrupt end to a consolidation push that saw Hafnia spend more than $500m building its position in Torm over the past year. Under the proposed exit, Hafnia shareholders would receive one Torm share for every 26.3 Hafnia shares held, with fractional entitlements settled in cash. items.summary: Trading in dry bulk forward freight agreements (FFAs) is heading for another record year, with volumes already approaching last year’s total as geopolitical upheaval drives greater demand for freight hedging. New analysis from Ursa Shipbrokers, using Baltic Exchange data, shows that 3.16m FFA lots changed hands between January and October, up 12% year-on-year and just shy of the 3.33m lots traded throughout 2025. The market has more than doubled in size since 2020, when annual turnover stood at 1.56m lots. Supramax contracts have recorded the fastest growth this year, with trading jumping 28.1% to 578,772 lots. Activity has subsequently moderated, although October’s 325,531 lots remained 17.4% above the corresponding month last year. The expanding market was a major talking point at this year’s Geneva Dry conference . “Liquidity in the market can only be good for it,” Karen Taylor, head of industrial commodities at ADM Investor Services, told delegates, highlighting how much easier it has become to trade FFAs compared with a decade ago. FFAs will form part of the discussion in the Risk Management In Dry Bulk panel at the 2027 edition of Geneva Dry on April 27. ICAP launched a dedicated global dry FFA desk in April, linking trading hubs in London, Copenhagen, Dubai and Singapore.

items.original_title: StealthGas crew airlifted from stricken LPG carrier off Bulgaria
items.summary: All 19 crewmembers of a StealthGas LPG carrier have been rescued after the vessel was caught up in a suspected drone attack off Bulgaria, the second serious merchant shipping incident in the western Black Sea in less than 24 hours. The Liberia-flagged, 7,500 cu m Gas Husky got into trouble overnight on Monday while sailing from Alexandria, Egypt, towards Romania’s Midia port. The 2012-built vessel disappeared from tracking systems shortly after midnight, with its emergency position-indicating radio beacon activated around 8 am local time on Tuesday. The 7,218 dwt fully pressurised LPG carrier forms part of Harry Vafias-led StealthGas’s fleet. The ship was approximately 14.5 nautical miles from the location where the Somali-flagged general cargo vessel Betul 8 capsized on Monday. That vessel, carrying around 3,000 tonnes of wheat from Romania to Egypt, was reportedly struck by two unmanned surface vessels before taking on water. All 12 crewmembers were rescued in an operation involving Bulgarian, Romanian and Turkish forces. Maritime security consultancy Diaplous has recorded at least 17 merchant vessels attacked off Romania and Bulgaria since mid-July, with several casualties reported in recent weeks. The latest incidents have occurred close to shipping routes used by vessels trading to and from Ukrainian and Romanian Black Sea ports.

items.original_title: Gemini carriers target complete return to Suez transits by mid-January
items.summary: Gemini Cooperation partners Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd will have made a full resumption of Suez transits on their Asia-Europe services by mid-January. Yesterday, the partners outlined the schedule for the last three Asia-North Europe services still detouring via the Cape of Good Hope to return to the Red Sea routing. The Asia-Northern Europe Loop 1 (Maersk AE2/Hapag-Lloyd NE1) will resume Suez transits in both directions with the departure of the 18,300 teu Mary Maersk from Ningbo on 4 December. The Asia-Northern Europe Loop 3 (Maersk AE3/Hapag-Lloyd NE3) will also fully resume westbound Suez transits following the departure of the 16,300 teu Alette Maersk from Shanghai on 20 December. Meanwhile, shippers on the Asia-Northern Europe Loop 2 (Maersk AE1/Hapag-Lloyd NE2), operated entirely by Hagag-Lloyd vessels, will have to wait until early 2027, with a full westbound resumption beginning with the departure of the 23,700 teu Damietta Express from Shanghai on 14 January, representing the last of Gemini’s Asia-Europe strings to return to Suez. It also remains to be seen how the widespread return to Suez routings will impact Asia-Europe schedule reliability, which according to Xeneta data, has fallen to historic lows – just 4% of vessels arrived on time in Europe ex-Asia in September, which rose to 7% in October.

items.title: African nations join forces to impose carbon charges on shipping
items.original_title: African nations join forces to impose carbon charges on shipping
items.summary: A growing group of African nations is pushing ahead with plans to introduce carbon charges on international shipping, raising the prospect of another regional emissions regime for shipowners already grappling with European environmental legislation. Guinea, Ivory Coast and Mauritania have signed an agreement at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, to develop a coordinated approach to charging ships for their carbon emissions. The initiative, promoted by the Africa Sovereign Carbon Registry Foundation (ASCRF), builds on existing schemes in Djibouti and Gabon, with the ambition of establishing a continent-wide framework for raising climate finance from international shipping and aviation. Under the model pioneered by Djibouti, vessels are charged $17 per tonne of CO2 calculated on 50% of emissions from voyages to and from the country’s ports. The latest agreement brings the number of countries associated with the proposed African coalition to six, although the status of Liberia’s involvement remains contentious. Monrovia stated earlier this year that it would not impose a unilateral carbon levy on international shipping. Other African countries are considering similar schemes. The development comes at a particularly sensitive moment for shipping’s decarbonisation negotiations, with the International Maritime Organization due to resume discussions on its proposed global emissions framework later this month.

Among those targeted are Dubai-based Lidoil DMCC, Spikoil DMCC, Lynx Ship Management, Stalwart Shipmanagement, Grace Shipmanagement and Greenlight Shipmanagement. The latest action follows Britain’s blacklisting of 11 additional vessels last week and comes amid intensifying European scrutiny of Russia’s international tanker operations. France and Britain will host an international conference in Paris on December 4 to coordinate further action against the shadow fleet. More than 670 vessels are already subject to EU port access and maritime services restrictions.

items.summary: The city’s great shipping families have survived every imaginable market shock. Keeping the next generation – and its capital – anchored in Hong Kong may prove a different challenge. Firoze Mirza, chairman of BSM Hong Kong, observes that several established families now have “third and fourth generations in the saddle”. Vikrant Gusain, chief executive of Dockendale Group, puts the succession challenge sharply: “Shipping therefore has to compete for family capital rather than assume it will inherit it.” More importantly, he argues, the next generation must be able to build a modern shipping enterprise in Hong Kong, not simply administer ships acquired by their parents or grandparents. Hong Kong-listed Pacific Basin moved strategic leadership and commercial decision-making to Singapore in 2025 amid US-China port-fee tensions, while Seaspan also relocated its headquarters to the city-state. The threat, therefore, is not an imminent extinction of Hong Kong’s shipping families. If the next generation continues to own vessels but chooses to finance, charter and direct them elsewhere, Hong Kong can retain impressive maritime statistics while losing some of the commercial influence that made those statistics possible.

items.original_title: Iron ore may rebound slightly as steel export orders improve
items.summary: The average imported iron ore margin rose from -7.71 yuan/mt to -5.90 yuan/mt in the latest period, with losses narrowing on higher spot prices for some products and lower seaborne premiums. On the supply side, SMM data showed iron ore inventories at 35 major Chinese ports stood at 152.12 million mt as of November 13, up 2.99 million mt week-on-week. Average daily port outbound volume fell 40,000 mt week-on-week to 3.08 million mt. On the demand side, SMM data showed total steel export orders in October at 3.3742 million mt, up 3.62% month-on-month and rising for the fourth consecutive month. Long steel orders rose 10.83% month-on-month to 1.7901 million mt. Given the usual lag between orders and shipments, steel exports may pick up month-on-month in November. Mill inquiries increased and traders held offers firm, weakening downward momentum in iron ore prices. Prices may halt their decline and rebound slightly in the near term, though high port inventories and environmental curbs are likely to cap the upside. The imported iron ore margin is likely to remain slightly negative, weighed down by rising ocean freight.

items.title: Singapore conventional bunker sales increased 13% in October
items.original_title: Singapore conventional bunker sales increased 13% in October
items.summary: Singapore’s total bunker sales rose in October, driven by increased sales across all fuel grades and a surge in vessel arrivals, according to preliminary data from the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA). Changes in bunker sales from September to October: • Total sales up 613,000 mt to 5.21 million mt • VLSFO sales up 365,000 mt to 2.58 million mt • HSFO sales up 208,000 mt to 2.20 million mt • MGO sales up 42,000 mt to 422,000 mt Sales of VLSFO, MGO and HSFO in Singapore increased by 16%, 11% and 10%, respectively, in October compared with September. The port recorded 4,008 vessel calls for bunkering during the month, up by 391 from September, taking activity to a multi-year high. Average stem sizes also edged up to around 1,300 mt, from approximately 1,270 mt a month earlier. Overall, Singapore’s total bunker sales in the first 10 months of the year were 4% higher than in the corresponding period last year. Fuel grade share of total sales in October (compared to year to date): • 50% VLSFO (50% YTD) • 42% HSFO (42% YTD) • 8% MGO (8% YTD) Source: By Tuhin Roy, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news/

items.title: Samsung Heavy Wins LNG Carrier Order
items.original_title: Samsung Heavy Wins LNG Carrier Order
items.summary: Samsung Heavy Industries said in a regulatory filing on Nov. 16 that it had won an order for one LNG carrier from a shipowner in Oceania for 342.4 billion won ($245.40 million). The vessel is scheduled to be delivered by July 2029. Including this latest order, Samsung Heavy Industries’ total orders for this year came to 49 vessels worth $12.7 billion. That amounts to 91% of its annual order target of $13.9 billion, meaning the company has moved past the final major hurdle toward achieving this year’s goal. In the offshore segment, two FLNG units worth $4.4 billion have served as a solid pillar supporting the overall performance. Samsung Heavy Industries secured orders for 47 vessels worth $8.3 billion in the commercial ship business alone this year, exceeding its original target of $5.7 billion by 146%. By vessel type, its portfolio was centered on high value-added ships, including 21 LNG carriers, including one LNG-FSRU, 14 crude oil carriers, six gas carriers, four container carriers, and two ethane carriers. A Samsung Heavy Industries official said, “Demand for LNG carriers is expected to maintain a solid trend,” adding, “We will further strengthen our order competitiveness by leveraging eco-friendly, high-efficiency LNG carriers.” Source: Business Korea

items.title: Why the carrier with the shortest terminal wait isn’t always the fastest option
items.original_title: Why the carrier with the shortest terminal wait isn’t always the fastest option
items.summary: The usual inputs to that decision are cost, space, and a general sense of which carrier “runs well” on a given route. Reliability gets discussed, but rarely checked against anything concrete, because container terminal performance data has not been easily compiled across carriers at the same set of ports. An example in Terminal Activity Using the Terminal Activity workspace in Container Intelligence, we can take four carrier groups calling San Pedro, Seattle, and Tacoma on vessels above 5,000 TEU, benchmarked against each other from January through September 2026: MSC is the dominant carrier at these ports by volume, with 122 terminal calls across the period, more than the other three carrier groups combined. China COSCO Shipping: 6.4 hours waiting plus 35.9 hours at berth, roughly 42 hours per call, the shortest total of the four. The carrier with the best waiting numbers has, by a wide margin, the longest total time in port once berth stay is counted. The carrier with the worst waiting rate, China COSCO Shipping, where 8 in 10 calls experience some wait, comes out with the shortest combined cycle, because both its waits and its berth stays run short.
